edges.effect_quant: In a 12-month sham-controlled trial of 493 adults with marked treatment-resistant depression, active vagus nerve stimulation did not beat sham on the primary MADRS time-in-response endpoint, but several secondary clinician- and patient-rated response measures favored active stimulation; in a 5-year registry of 795 patients, cumulative response was 67.6% with adjunctive vagus nerve stimulation versus 40.9% with treatment as usual, and remission was 43.3% versus 25.7%.
edges.population: adults with severe or marked treatment-resistant major depressive episodes, including long-duration unipolar and bipolar depression treated with adjunctive vagus nerve stimulation
edges.mechanism: Vagus nerve stimulation may alter afferent signaling to limbic and monoaminergic circuits, reshape norepinephrine and serotonin tone, and promote neuroplasticity in networks that remain dysregulated after multiple failed antidepressant treatments.
edges.summary: The human literature suggests that vagus nerve stimulation can help a subset of people with treatment-resistant depression, but the effect is slower and less uniform than the early enthusiasm implied. The strongest long-term signal is favorable, yet the large sham-controlled trial showed a more complicated picture with secondary benefits but a negative primary endpoint.
edges.caveats: Most benefit estimates come from adjunctive-treatment settings rather than clean monotherapy comparisons. Selection effects, expectancy, and the slow-onset nature of neuromodulation make it harder to interpret observational gains, and even the large randomized trial did not show superiority on its primary MADRS endpoint.
